output.brief: The enrolment drop is mainly a pricing effect, not an Admissions Office failure. Applications, admits and student quality all rose. Yield fell only in the tiers whose scholarships were cut: Dean's went from $14,000 to $9,000 and yield fell from 45.2% to 31.9%. Merit went from $9,000 to $5,000 and yield fell from 44.9% to 32.3%. Presidential awards were unchanged, and yield there was flat at about 36%. The no-award group was also nearly flat, at 38.5% to 37.0%. Early action ran on the old system and on time, yet its yield fell about as much as regular decision (7.4 points against 7.5). So the late regular-decision answers don't explain the drop, although they hurt some individual students, as Gareth Pell's email shows. I didn't check whether the portal lost documents, and I didn't separate the effect of the frozen reader posts from that of the unstable scoring module. I'm fairly confident in the main finding, and the sample is large. Next steps: don't replace the director on this basis. Take a proposal to the finance committee to restore awards in the Dean's and Merit tiers, with the revenue trade-off modelled, before award letters go out. Also set a regular-decision turnaround target, and check the missing-transcript reports before ordering any vendor rebuild.
